Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

0 · Kickoff, all cells together

Team: a team lead plus one or more people per cell. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who gathers the cell's files and sends one roll-up to the team lead.

  • P1
    Written authorization: hosts and subnets in scope, change approver, change window, and the owner to call. Note the start time.
  • P1
    Required-services list from the owner: each business app, its host, port, and users; remote access and vendor links. Every step that names the required list reads from this list.
  • P1
    Split each cell's hosts among its people: list them in the cell's Hosts bar with who holds each, and name a cell lead in each cell of three or more.
  • P1
    Agree on management subnets, jump host, NTP source, and syslog collector (the Cisco cell builds ACLs from these).
  • P1
    Team vault for every new secret, plus one shared change log. Sync points: kickoff done · credentials cut over · firewall and ACL changes announced · freeze (the team lead sets the times on the Collab Tab).
  • P1
    Departed admins: names, named accounts, shared accounts they used, and devices they held.
  • P1
    Secrets the old team knew, each with an owner cell; rotate in Phase 3:
SecretCell
AD admins, krbtgt, DSRM, service accounts, local Administrator, backup console, RADIUS shared secretsWindows
root / sudo / wheel, SSH keys, database and app secrets*nix
enable and device users, SNMP, TACACS+/RADIUS keys, VPN pre-shared keys, Wi-Fi keysCisco
hypervisor hosts, BMC (out-of-band management), NAS, ISP and domain-registrar portals, cloud and email admins, security and remote-management consolesassign at kickoff

Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

Windows Takeover Checklist

Windows 11 (24H2–25H2) · Windows Server 2022 / 2025 · Active Directory. For the Windows cell of a takeover team (a team lead plus one or more people per cell; a cell of three or more names a cell lead) inheriting a network whose last admin team left under a negligence finding.

Situation. Treat every secret the old team held as known to outsiders, and every setting as unreviewed. Work in an elevated PowerShell 5.1 window.

Solo: domain first (it reaches every host), P1 lines in order, P2 when on schedule. Cell of two or more: split the hosts in the Hosts bar, one person on the domain and DCs and the others on servers and workstations; each person reads the line aloud, logs the change, and checks the → read-back. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who sends the cell's roll-up to the team lead.

Key: P1 = inside the team clock · P2 = when on schedule · P3 = week-1 plan · → = expected read-back · <x> = your value · GUI+ = the GUI is faster here · ⚠︎ and an orange bar = untested on a real system: use with caution, at your own risk · a line without them = run cleanly on a real system.

Rules: evidence before change · disable before delete · a console session (VM console or BMC) stays open for any remote-access change · keep every required service running · one change, one log line (time, host, change, old → new, undo).

1 · Evidence and safety net (read-only)

  • P1
    Safety net per server: a VM checkpoint from the hypervisor console, or a confirmed backup from last night.
  • P1
    Inventory (on a DC): flag unsupported systems (Windows 10 outside ESU; Server 2016 support ends Jan 12, 2027) and stale computers.
    Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties OperatingSystem,LastLogonDate | Sort LastLogonDate | ft Name,OperatingSystem,LastLogonDate1⚠︎
  • P1
    Transcript on every host you touch (records each command and its output):
    New-Item C:\takeover -ItemType Directory -Force; Start-Transcript C:\takeover\$env:COMPUTERNAME.txt -Append2 3⚠︎
  • P1
    Snapshot block, every host (paste; DCs skip the two local-account lines):
    cd C:\takeover; Get-LocalUser | Export-Csv users.csv -NoType; net localgroup Administrators > admins.txt4 5⚠︎
    Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Export-Csv listen.csv -NoType; Get-Service | Export-Csv svc.csv -NoType6 7⚠︎
    Get-ScheduledTask | Export-Csv tasks.csv -NoType; Get-SmbShare | Export-Csv shares.csv -NoType; Get-MpPreference > defender.txt8 9 10⚠︎
    secedit /export /cfg C:\takeover\secpol.inf; auditpol /backup /file:C:\takeover\audit.csv; wevtutil epl Security Security.evtx; wevtutil epl System System.evtx11 12 13⚠︎
  • P1
    Domain block (one DC):
    Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties whenCreated,LastLogonDate,PasswordLastSet,PasswordNeverExpires,AdminCount | Export-Csv ad-users.csv -NoType14⚠︎
    'Domain Admins','Enterprise Admins','Schema Admins','Administrators','Account Operators','Backup Operators','Server Operators','DnsAdmins','Group Policy Creator Owners' | % { $g=$_; Get-ADGroupMember $g -Recursive | select @{n='Group';e={$g}},SamAccountName } | Export-Csv priv.csv -NoType15⚠︎
    mkdir gpo; Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\takeover\gpo; Get-GPO -All | Sort ModificationTime -Desc | select -First 15 DisplayName,ModificationTime16 17⚠︎
    repadmin /replsummary > repl.txt; dcdiag /q > dcdiag.txt18 19⚠︎
  • P1
    Who is signed in now: quser20⚠︎ on each server; file servers Get-SmbSession | ft ClientUserName,ClientComputerName21⚠︎.
  • P1
    Record signs of misuse (unknown admins, remote-control tools, Defender exclusions, accounts created in the last 90 days) and escalate per policy before cleanup. Hash the folder and copy it to the team share:
    $h = Get-ChildItem C:\takeover -File -Recurse | ? Name -ne "$env:COMPUTERNAME.txt" | Get-FileHash; $h | Export-Csv C:\takeover\hashes.csv -NoType22 23⚠︎

2 · Start the long jobs

Domain: start the "Takeover Baseline – Workstations" GPO here, linked at the workstation OUs (or filtered to workstations), so servers and DCs stay outside it. The update-blocker, local-group, Windows LAPS, Defender, firewall, RDP, and SMB settings join it as you reach them, with the Guest account status at Disabled (Security Options), and domain policy carries them to every workstation at the next refresh. A policy left unconfigured leaves a value written by hand on a host in place, so these settings undo local tampering only when set explicitly: Defender's local administrator merge behavior for lists at Disabled (exclusions added through Set-MpPreference on a host stop applying); Defender's Path, Extension, and Process Exclusions set explicitly (Enabled with the approved entries alone, or Disabled), since exclusions written by hand under the Policies key read as policy; Defender's "Turn off Microsoft Defender Antivirus" and "Turn off real-time protection" at Disabled; Windows Update's intranet update location (Disabled, or Enabled with your own WSUS server) with automatic updates on; and the Windows Update service (wuauserv) at Manual under System Services. Servers and DCs, and the other workstation steps, run host by host or through remote shells; with domain policy alone, the hands-on sample takes those other workstation steps by hand, the workstations past it take the Phase 3 cut-off from this GPO on the day (the listed local accounts disabled, the listed remote-control tools blocked by inbound and outbound firewall rules, and a restart, targeted to leave out the sample, that ends live sessions), and their remaining steps go into the week-1 plan. With only a few workstations past the sample, taking the cut-off by hand on them can finish sooner than building these pieces; the estimate's Workstations list says which it counts.

  • P1
    Update blockers: reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate /s24⚠︎ → an unexplained WUServer or NoAutoUpdate=1 is a finding; delete it (Phase 1 saved the state). Then Set-Service wuauserv -StartupType Manual; Start-Service wuauserv25 26⚠︎.
  • P1
    GUI+ Settings > Windows Update27 > Check for updates (Server Core: sconfig28⚠︎, option 6). Restarts wait for Phase 8 or the change window.
  • P1
    WSUS server, when present: the Oct 23, 2025 out-of-band update or later is installed (CVE-2025-59287, actively exploited), and TCP 8530/8531 stay internal.
  • P1
    Defender: Update-MpSignature; Start-MpScan -ScanType QuickScan -AsJob29 30⚠︎ (Server without Defender: Install-WindowsFeature Windows-Defender31⚠︎). → Get-MpComputerStatus | fl AMRunningMode,RealTimeProtectionEnabled,IsTamperProtected32 shows Normal, True, and True on Windows 11 (servers report tamper protection True only under central Defender management). A third-party EDR puts Defender in Passive; confirm that EDR console logs in as your team.

3 · Cut off the old team

Domain (whoever holds the DCs)

  • P1
    Disable each departed admin's accounts now; delete after the HR/legal hold. Disable-ADAccount <sam>33⚠︎ → (Get-ADUser <sam>).Enabled14⚠︎ is False.
  • P1
    Privileged groups hold the approved list only (read priv.csv): Remove-ADGroupMember '<group>' -Members <sam> -Confirm:$false34⚠︎. Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins stay empty apart from one break-glass account.
  • P1
    New vault passwords for every remaining privileged account, the built-in Administrator (RID 500), and shared admin accounts:
    Set-ADAccountPassword <sam> -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'New password')35⚠︎
  • P1
    krbtgt reset 1 of 2 (voids forged tickets), once repadmin /replsummary18⚠︎ shows zero failures. AD swaps whatever you type for a strong random value; each read-only DC has its own krbtgt_<number>. Reset 2 goes in the week-1 plan, at least 10 hours later.
    Set-ADAccountPassword krbtgt -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString 'Any value')35⚠︎
  • P1
    DSRM password, each DC: ntdsutil "set dsrm password" "reset password on server null" q q36⚠︎.
  • P1
    Service accounts: rotate each one whose service you can update today (set the new password on that service right after); list the rest with owners for week 1.
    Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -like '*'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet | ft Name,PasswordLastSet14⚠︎
  • P1
    Rotate the rest of your kickoff rows: backup console, RADIUS shared secrets (with the Cisco cell), and any hypervisor or BMC rows assigned to you.

Every host (each person on their own hosts)

  • P1
    Local Administrators and Remote Desktop Users hold the approved list only (an orphaned SID makes the cmdlet fail; net localgroup Administrators5 still lists the group):
    Get-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-544; Get-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-55537⚠︎
    Remove-LocalGroupMember -SID S-1-5-32-544 -Member '<name>'38⚠︎
  • P1
    Local Administrator password: Windows LAPS hosts Reset-LapsPassword39⚠︎; others Get-LocalUser | ? SID -like '*-500' | Set-LocalUser -Password (Read-Host -AsSecureString)4 40⚠︎ host by host, each with a password of its own for the vault (one run of that line across hosts would give every host the same password). Workstations that domain policy reaches take the Windows LAPS policy in the workstation baseline (once per domain: the LAPS schema update and the computers' permission to update their own passwords on their OU); each then sets and backs up a password of its own at its next policy refresh, and one that already holds a LAPS password rotates at that refresh once an admin session with the LAPS module and directory rights sets its LAPS password expiration to now (the line below). Through remote shells, the LAPS reset runs on the LAPS hosts in one pass. Guest stays off: Get-LocalUser | ? SID -like '*-501' | Disable-LocalUser4 41⚠︎.
    DomainSet-LapsADPasswordExpirationTime -Identity <computer>42⚠︎
  • P1
    Enabled local accounts are known and password-protected: Get-LocalUser | ? Enabled | ft Name,PasswordRequired,LastLogon4 → Disable-LocalUser <name>41⚠︎ for the rest. With domain policy alone, the workstations past the hands-on sample take this cut-off from the workstation baseline on the day: a Group Policy Preferences Local Users and Groups item for each account the sample flags, action Update with "Account is disabled" checked (Update also creates that account, disabled, on a host that lacks it).
  • P1
    End the old team's live sessions: quser20⚠︎ → logoff <ID>43⚠︎; file servers Close-SmbSession -ClientUserName '<DOMAIN\user>' -Force44⚠︎. With domain policy alone, the workstation baseline ends the sessions on the workstations past the hands-on sample on the day: a Group Policy Preferences immediate task, set to apply once, with item-level targeting that leaves out the hands-on sample's computers (a Computer Name item set to Is Not for each, joined with AND), restarts each workstation past the sample at its next policy refresh, which signs every user out, so tell the staff first. The old team's domain accounts are disabled earlier in this phase and the listed local accounts by the step above, so they stay signed out.
  • P1
    Remote-control tools the old team could reach you through (installed programs and services):
    $rx='AnyDesk|ScreenConnect|ConnectWise|TeamViewer|Splashtop|Atera|NetSupport|Remote ?Utilities|RemotePC|Kaseya|N-?able|Pulseway|GoTo|LogMeIn|Zoho|BeyondTrust|Bomgar|SimpleHelp|JWrapper|RustDesk|Ninja|Radmin|VNC|ngrok'⚠︎
    Get-ItemProperty HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*,HKLM:\Software\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\*,Registry::HKEY_USERS\*\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall\* -EA 0 | ? DisplayName -match $rx | ft DisplayName,InstallDate45⚠︎
    Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | ? { "$($_.Name) $($_.DisplayName) $($_.PathName)" -match $rx } | ft Name,State,PathName46⚠︎
    Get-Process | ? { "$($_.Name) $($_.Path)" -match $rx } | ft Name,Id,Path47⚠︎
    → uninstall each one the owner leaves out (winget uninstall --name '<name>'48⚠︎, or Settings > Apps49); portable copies show only as processes, so delete their folders too. A sanctioned tool gets a new account in your name. With domain policy alone, the workstation baseline cuts the tools the sample finds off the network on the workstations past it on the day, and the week-1 plan uninstalls them: an inbound and an outbound Windows Defender Firewall block rule for each of the tool's program paths (its service and its client). A block rule overrides allow rules (all but authenticated-bypass ones, set to override block rules), so it also stops the inbound allow rules a tool's installer added; it holds on every Windows edition and covers a tool's service that runs as SYSTEM; an AppLocker deny rule, enforced on every Windows 11 edition once the Application Identity service starts automatically, covers such a service only with services enforcement set in its policy XML.
  • P1
    SSH server keys (Server 2025 ships the SSH server): Get-Service sshd -EA 07⚠︎; keep only the keys you can attribute in C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys and C:\Users\*\.ssh\authorized_keys.

For each unsigned or unknown entry: note path and hash, untick it, and delete after evidence. CLI record: autorunsc64 -accepteula -nobanner -a * -s -h -m -c * > C:\takeover\autoruns.csv50⚠︎.

5 · Shrink exposure

Announce firewall and RDP changes at the firewall and ACL sync; work from the console for these.

  • P1
    Firewall on, inbound blocked by default: Set-NetFirewallProfile -All -Enabled True -DefaultInboundAction Block -DefaultOutboundAction Allow60⚠︎ → Get-NetFirewallProfile | ft Name,Enabled,DefaultInboundAction61.
  • P1
    Custom inbound allow rules (built-in rules carry a Group): Get-NetFirewallRule -Enabled True -Direction Inbound -Action Allow | ? {-not $_.Group} | ft Name,DisplayName,Profile62 → Disable-NetFirewallRule -Name '<name>'63⚠︎ for each one off the required list. GUI+ wf.msc64 sorts by program.
  • P1
    RDP off where unused: Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server' fDenyTSConnections 1; Disable-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup 'Remote Desktop'65 63⚠︎. Where required: NLA on and source-scoped:
    Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp' UserAuthentication 165⚠︎
    Set-NetFirewallRule -DisplayGroup 'Remote Desktop' -RemoteAddress <mgmt-subnet>66⚠︎
  • P1

6 · Policy and visibility

Domain: the audit, log, credential-theft, and UAC settings suit every host, so they go in a new GPO, "Takeover Baseline", linked at the domain (GUI+ gpmc.msc56; it reaches every host at the next refresh). Workgroup hosts take the lines host by host or through remote shells.

  • P1
    Password and lockout (14 characters; length beats complexity, and changes follow events, such as today's):
    Set-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy <domain> -MinPasswordLength 14 -ComplexityEnabled $true -PasswordHistoryCount 24 -MinPasswordAge 1.00:00:00 -MaxPasswordAge 365.00:00:00 -LockoutThreshold 5 -LockoutDuration 00:30:00 -LockoutObservationWindow 00:30:00 -ReversibleEncryptionEnabled $false79⚠︎
    Localnet accounts /minpwlen:14 /uniquepw:24 /minpwage:1 /maxpwage:36580⚠︎
    Localnet accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:30 /lockoutwindow:3081⚠︎
  • P2
    Fine-grained password policies override the domain policy for their groups; each one meets the same floor: Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy -Filter * | ft Name,MinPasswordLength,AppliesTo82⚠︎.

    Advanced audit policy (DCs and servers first):

    auditpol --% /set /subcategory:"Credential Validation","User Account Management","Logon","Sensitive Privilege Use","Other Object Access Events" /success:enable /failure:enable83⚠︎
    auditpol --% /set /subcategory:"Security Group Management","Process Creation","Special Logon","Audit Policy Change","Authentication Policy Change" /success:enable83⚠︎

    DomainGet-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'; Get-ADDefaultDomainPasswordPolicy; auditpol /get /category:*15 94 95⚠︎
  • P1
    The owner confirms each required service with a real user: sign-in, file shares, apps, printing, and remote access.
  • P1
    Restarts for updates, LSA protection, and features: one server at a time, DCs one at a time, inside the window; recheck required services after each.
  • P1
    Hand off: change log, vault entries, findings, and the week-1 plan; then Stop-Transcript96⚠︎.

Week-1 plan

  • P3
    krbtgt reset 2 of 2, at least 10 hours after reset 1 and after replication.
  • P3
    Windows LAPS on every server and on each host the workstation baseline left out; separate admin accounts per tier; admins in Protected Users; MFA for remote access and email.
  • P3
    Group Managed Service Accounts for services; retire unsupported systems; a monthly patch cadence.
  • P3
    The vendor's security baseline for each Windows version, piloted in one OU; attack surface reduction rules; Credential Guard; BitLocker with escrowed keys; Administrator protection on Windows 11 desktops outside LAPS.
  • P3
    Secure Boot 2023 certificates on every host before the 2011 ones expire: HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecureBoot\Servicing → UEFICA2023Status = Updated (System log event 1808).
  • P3
    Central log collection (Windows Event Forwarding or a SIEM); rerun the Phase 4 domain checks and track each finding to closed.
  • P3
    Workstations past the hands-on sample: the Phase 1 and 4 evidence and hunting steps; where domain policy alone reached them, also the steps it leaves to this plan: the snapshots (taken after the baseline, so they record its result; the sample's snapshots, taken before it, show what it changed), the Windows Update check, the Defender signature update and scan, the Phase 3 reads (live sessions, local accounts, and remote-control tools) with uninstalling the tools the baseline blocks, the custom inbound-rule review, roles and features removal, and read-backs. Each goes host by host or from the reach runs' collected output, with each finding tracked to closed.

Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

*nix Takeover Checklist

Debian 12 / 13 and derivatives · RHEL 9 / 10 and Fedora · SLES 15 / 16, openSUSE Leap, and Tumbleweed · FreeBSD 14.x / 15.x · OpenBSD 7.9 / 8.0 · OpenIndiana Hipster and OmniOS · Oracle Solaris 11.4 · macOS 26 / 27. For the *nix cell of a takeover team (a team lead plus one or more people per cell; a cell of three or more names a cell lead) inheriting a network whose last admin team left under a negligence finding.

Situation. Treat every secret the old team held as known to outsiders, and every setting as unreviewed. Pick the host's family with the family switch, or print that family's copy; each step then shows that family's lines. Run each line in a root shell.

Debian Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎, or su -2⚠︎ on hosts installed with a root password (those ship without sudo).

RHEL Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎ as a member of wheel.

SUSE Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎ or su -2⚠︎. On 15.x and on upgraded hosts, sudo asks for root's password; fresh 16.x and Tumbleweed installs (sudo-policy-wheel-auth-self) ask wheel members for their own.

FreeBSD Root shell: su -2⚠︎; when echo $0⚠︎ names csh or tcsh (hosts upgraded from 13.x keep it), run exec env SHELL=/bin/sh /bin/sh -l3⚠︎ first, since every FreeBSD line is written for sh.

OpenBSD Root shell: su -l2⚠︎ as a member of wheel, or doas -s4⚠︎ where doas.conf permits it; root's shell is ksh, and every OpenBSD line is written for sh and ksh.

illumos Root shell: su -2⚠︎; root's login shell is bash on OpenIndiana and OmniOS, and every illumos line also runs in ksh93.

Solaris Root shell: su -2⚠︎ (root is a role: each admin who holds it signs in as themselves, then assumes it); every Solaris line runs in bash and ksh93.

macOS Root shell: sudo -i1⚠︎ as an admin, while the root account stays disabled; Phase 1 gives Terminal Full Disk Access first.

Labels: Debian = Debian 12/13 and derivatives · RHEL = RHEL 9/10 and Fedora · SUSE = SLES 15/16, openSUSE Leap, and Tumbleweed · FreeBSD = FreeBSD 14/15 · OpenBSD = OpenBSD 7.9/8.0 · illumos = OpenIndiana Hipster and OmniOS · Solaris = Oracle Solaris 11.4 · macOS = macOS 26/27 · Linux = the three Linux families · BSD = FreeBSD and OpenBSD · Unix = illumos and Solaris. In All, a badge names each line's family, and a line without a badge fits every family.

Solo: internet-facing servers first, P1 lines in order, P2 when on schedule. Cell of two or more: split the hosts in the Hosts bar by family (Linux and FreeBSD, say) or by role (servers and desktops), each person with the switch set to the family of the host in front of them; each reads the line aloud, logs the change, and checks the → read-back. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who sends the cell's roll-up to the team lead.

Key: P1 = inside the team clock · P2 = when on schedule · P3 = week-1 plan · → = expected read-back · <x> = your value · GUI+ = the GUI is faster here · ⚠︎ and an orange bar = untested on a real system: use with caution, at your own risk · a line without them = run cleanly on a real system.

Rules: evidence before change · lock before delete · a console session (VM console or BMC) stays open for any SSH, PAM, sudo, or firewall change · keep every required service running · one change, one log line (time, host, change, old → new, undo).

1 · Evidence and safety net (read-only)

  • P1
    A second root shell stays open until the end: your way back after an SSH, PAM, or sudo mistake.
    Unix → the system console counts as that second shell, and it is also the way back after an RBAC mistake.
    macOS → macOS keeps the root account disabled, so the way back is a second admin Terminal with sudo -i1⚠︎ open, or the recovery environment (the console password unlocks it). sudo -i1⚠︎ starts root's own /bin/sh, where every macOS line here runs as written; in a zsh shell (sudo -s1⚠︎ keeps the admin's zsh), run setopt nonomatch5⚠︎ first, since zsh otherwise stops a whole line when one of its wildcards matches nothing.
    macOS → before the snapshot, give Terminal Full Disk Access (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access) and log that change in the session log: with it, root's reads of protected folders under /Users, the privacy database, and the logs come back whole.
  • P1
    Safety net before any change: a VM snapshot, or the host's own restore point:
    Debiantimeshift --create --comments pre-takeover6⚠︎(hosts with timeshift)
    RHELbtrfs subvolume snapshot -r / /pre-takeover7⚠︎(Fedora on btrfs)
    RHELlvcreate -s -L 5G -n pre-takeover <vg>/<root-lv>8⚠︎(RHEL on LVM with free space: vgs9⚠︎ shows VFree)
    SUSEsnapper create -p -d pre-takeover10⚠︎(btrfs root with a root config in snapper list-configs10⚠︎; log the printed number)
    FreeBSDbectl create pre-takeover11⚠︎(FreeBSD on ZFS)
    illumosbeadm create pre-takeover12⚠︎
    Solarisbeadm create pre-takeover; zfs snapshot -r rpool/export@pre-takeover; zfs snapshot -r rpool/VARSHARE@pre-takeover12 13⚠︎(a clone of the running boot environment, plus the home folders and the shared /var data14, which sit outside it)
    macOStmutil localsnapshot15⚠︎
    SUSE → root snapshots leave /home, /opt, /srv, /var, and /usr/local aside, so a VM snapshot stays first choice for data.
    RHEL → the Fedora snapshot leaves /home (its own subvolume) aside, so a VM snapshot stays first choice for data there too.
    OpenBSD → the safety net is a VM snapshot (FFS keeps one live copy of each file); on bare metal, the snapshot block's etc.tgz and /var/backups (security(8)16's copies of each file in /etc/changelist17, run nightly by daily(8)) hold the configuration, and /altroot holds yesterday's root file system where /etc/daily.local sets ROOTBACKUP=1 and /etc/fstab carries an altroot line.
    illumos → a boot environment copies the root file system, /var included; /export (homes) and other pools stay outside it, so a VM snapshot stays first choice for data.
    Solaris → beadm list12⚠︎ shows pre-takeover, and zfs list -t snapshot -r rpool/export rpool/VARSHARE18⚠︎ shows the home and shared /var snapshots. A boot environment holds the OS datasets alone, so data pools stay outside it and a VM snapshot stays first choice for data.
    macOS → an APFS local snapshot you can restore from in the recovery environment; a Time Machine backup to an external disk is the fuller restore point and stays first choice for data.
  • P1
    Session log (records each command and its output):
    Linux · BSD · Unixmkdir -m 700 -p /root/takeover && cd /root/takeover && script -a session.log19⚠︎
    macOSmkdir -m 700 -p /var/root/takeover && cd /var/root/takeover && script -a session.log19⚠︎
  • P1
    Snapshot block (paste per host):
    Linux{ uname -a; cat /etc/os-release; } > sys.txt; ss -tulpn > listen.txt; ps auxwwf > ps.txt; getent passwd > passwd.txt; getent group > group.txt20 21 22 23⚠︎
    Linuxsystemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled > enabled.txt; systemctl list-timers --all > timers.txt; { last -Faiw || lslogins; } > last.txt 2>&124 25 26⚠︎

    OpenBSD → put the line right below the line that opens the default class (default:\) in /etc/login.conf. With passwordtries at 0, passwd(1) accepts a new password only once it passes the check (the stock 3 enforces it three times, then accepts). A class file in /etc/login.conf.d takes precedence over the same class in login.conf, so a lower value there is a finding. A spare account's own passwd107⚠︎ refuses a 10-character password.
    illumos → pam_authtok_check reads /etc/default/passwd266 at each password change, and root's resets meet the length check too once force_check is on (a pam.conf line then ends pam_authtok_check.so.1 force_check267); test with root running passwd <spare>107⚠︎ and a 10-character password, which is refused. A dictionary check needs DICTIONLIST=<word file> in the same file, then mkpwdict268⚠︎ builds its database. A CRYPT_DEFAULT of __unix__ cuts passwords at 8 characters, so it is a finding.
    Solaris → once its passwd stencil is on, the account-policy195 service writes /etc/default/passwd from its properties and holds the policy, so later changes go through svccfg; the stock rules stay (2 letters and 1 non-letter at least). Root holds solaris.* (which includes solaris.passwd.nocheck), so resets done as root skip these checks: each reset uses a 14-character vault password, and each user's own change meets the policy (getent user_attr | egrep 'solaris\.(\*|passwd\.nocheck)'23⚠︎ lists each account granted either one directly). A default of __unix__ caps passwords at eight characters: svccfg -s account-policy setprop password/crypt/default = 655⚠︎, then svcadm refresh account-policy157⚠︎, and each affected user resets their password. The Phase 1 copy of /etc keeps the old file for any setting the owner wants back (HISTORY, say).
    macOS → -setaccountpolicies replaces the whole set, so the lockout step below rewrites this file with both rules. The rule applies at each account's next password change. A Mac under MDM gets it from the passcode settings declaration (MinimumLength 14) instead.

    macOS → macOS randomizes every process's address space by itself, and System Integrity Protection guards system processes against debugging (the access-control step below reads it).

7 · Recovery readiness

  • P1
    Backups: the job, its last success, an offline copy, and repository keys rotated. Look in cron and timers for the job, then list its restore points with the backup tool:
    Debiantimeshift --list6⚠︎(hosts with timeshift)
    RHELbtrfs subvolume list -s / 2>/dev/null; lvs7 327⚠︎(Fedora btrfs snapshots, RHEL LVM snapshots)
    SUSEsnapper list10⚠︎
    FreeBSDzfs list -t snapshot -o name,creation -s creation | tail18⚠︎
    OpenBSDcrontab -l; cat /etc/daily.local /etc/weekly.local /etc/monthly.local 2>/dev/null51⚠︎→ the backup job and its schedule; each other line has a reason, and SUIDSKIP and PASSWDSKIP stay unset or list approved entries alone
    illumosbeadm list; zfs list -t snapshot -o name,creation -s creation | tail12 18⚠︎

    macOStmutil destinationinfo; tmutil latestbackup; tmutil listlocalsnapshots /15⚠︎→ a destination by name and a backup from last night (latestbackup reads a mounted destination)

    OpenBSD → ROOTBACKUP=1328 in /etc/daily.local, with an /altroot line in /etc/fstab, refreshes a backup root file system each night: a local restore point, so the offline copy stays its own check. A dump(8)329 archive lists its files with restore -t -f <dump-file>330⚠︎.
    Unix → boot environments and snapshots on the same pool are restore points; the backup job with its offline copy is its own check.
    macOS → the job lives in Time Machine or in launchd (launchctl list61⚠︎); a reply that names Full Disk Access means the shell lacks it (GUI+ System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access; over SSH, Remote Login's full disk access setting).

    Post-change restore point (a VM snapshot, or the host's own):

    RHELbtrfs subvolume snapshot -r / /post-takeover7⚠︎(Fedora on btrfs)

8 · Verify, freeze, hand off

From the freeze, verify and log only.

  • P1
    Reboot where updates need it, one host at a time, console open:
    Debiancat /run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null; needrestart -b -k 2>/dev/null; uname -r; ls -1v /boot/vmlinuz-* | tail -1163 20⚠︎→ the newest vmlinuz name ends in the uname -r value, or NEEDRESTART-KSTA: 1

    FreeBSDfreebsd-version -kru38⚠︎(installed kernel newer than the running one)
    OpenBSDls -lt /var/syspatch | head -5; sysctl kern.boottime42⚠︎→ a patch folder dated after the boot time whose errata entry fixes the kernel (openbsd.org/errata80.html332, errata79.html) means reboot

    Solarisbeadm list; uname -v; pkg list entire12 20 52⚠︎→ an R on a boot environment other than the N one means reboot (NR on one line means the running one boots next); after the reboot svcs -x49⚠︎ prints nothing
    macOSsoftwareupdate --install '<label>' --restart85⚠︎(each label Phase 2 downloaded; on Apple silicon it asks for a volume owner's password)

    Unix → pkg update -r92⚠︎ copies the running system at the moment it runs, so the session log's tail and this step's output stay in the old boot environment: after the reboot, beadm mount <old-be> /mnt && cp -p /mnt/root/takeover/session.log /root/takeover/session-pre-reboot.log && beadm unmount <old-be>12 30⚠︎ keeps them, and cd /root/takeover && script -a session.log19⚠︎ starts logging again before the read-backs.

Week-1 plan

  • P3
    Central logging; SSH keys only, through a bastion with MFA; one configuration-management tool so hosts stay identical.
  • P3
    A host audit tool for a ranked follow-up list, and a file-integrity baseline:
    Debian → the packaged aide builds the baseline (aideinit335⚠︎).
    RHEL → dnf install aide && aide --init33 336⚠︎, then move /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz to aide.db.gz; application allow-listing (fapolicyd), a USB device policy (usbguard), and a boot-loader password (grub2-setpassword337⚠︎) round out the plan.
    SUSE → zypper in aide && aide --init && mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db37 336 156⚠︎, then aide --check336⚠︎ reads the baseline (16.x and Tumbleweed: systemctl enable --now aide.timer24⚠︎ runs it daily; 15.x: copy the package's example /usr/share/doc/packages/aide/examples/etc/cron.daily/aide.sh into /etc/cron.daily/). Setting PERMISSION_SECURITY="secure local" in /etc/sysconfig/security and running chkstat --system --set210⚠︎ drops SUID from some tools, so test it first.
    FreeBSD → mtree for the baseline; FreeBSD securelevel once updates settle.
    OpenBSD → security(8)16, run nightly by daily(8), mails root the setuid changes and the diffs of /etc/changelist and /etc/mtree/special; a baseline per tree joins that run: mtree -cx -p /bin -K sha256digest,type > /etc/mtree/bin.secure74⚠︎, then /sbin, /usr/bin, /usr/sbin, and /usr/local/bin, each followed by chmod 600290⚠︎. Securelevel 2275 stays aside while pf rules still change, since it freezes them.
    illumos → BART builds the file-integrity baseline: bart create > <manifest>338⚠︎ catalogs the root file system, and a later manifest with bart compare <control> <test>338⚠︎ lists each change; pkg verify52⚠︎ checks every packaged file against its package.
    Solaris → pkg install security/compliance166⚠︎, then compliance assess -b solaris -p Recommended -a week1339⚠︎ and compliance report -a week1339⚠︎ rank the follow-up list; bart create -R /etc > /root/takeover/bart-etc.manifest338⚠︎ records the file-integrity baseline (bart compare338⚠︎ reads a later manifest against it), and pkg verify52⚠︎ checks every packaged file.
    macOS → the signed system volume seals the OS itself (csrutil authenticated-root status63⚠︎ reads enabled); mtree -c -K sha256digest -p /Library > /var/root/takeover/library.mtree74⚠︎ and mtree -c -K sha256digest -p /private/etc > /var/root/takeover/etc.mtree74⚠︎ baseline the writable trees; copy both to the evidence store, and the week-1 plan compares /private/etc against that copy each week (mtree -f <evidence-store>/etc.mtree -p /private/etc74⚠︎ names each changed file, sudoers and pam.d included). A firmware password (Intel) or Recovery Lock (Apple silicon, set through MDM) keeps recoveryOS for the team.
  • P3
    Linux · macOS Hosts with mandatory access control disabled come back to enforcing, one host at a time with the owner's sign-off:
    RHEL · SUSE → SELinux: SELINUX=permissive in /etc/selinux/config, clear selinux=0 from the boot flags, fixfiles -F onboot333⚠︎, reboot (the relabel is slow), read the AVCs, then enforcing.
    SUSE → SELinux on SUSE also needs update-bootloader --add-option security=selinux304⚠︎ and update-bootloader --add-option selinux=1304⚠︎, then update-bootloader --config304⚠︎.
    Debian · SUSE → AppArmor: clear apparmor=0 (and any lsm= list that leaves apparmor out) from the boot flags, reboot, then aa-enforce301⚠︎ each profile the owner's tests pass.
    macOS → System Integrity Protection: start up in recoveryOS (Apple silicon: hold the power button; Intel: Command-R), open Terminal there, run csrutil enable63⚠︎, then restart; csrutil status63⚠︎ reads enabled. Authenticated Root disabled: in recoveryOS run csrutil authenticated-root enable63⚠︎, and boot the last sealed snapshot (bless --mount <system volume> --last-sealed-snapshot340⚠︎) once the owner has saved any change made to the system volume; csrutil authenticated-root status63⚠︎ then reads enabled. An unapproved boot-args clears with nvram -d boot-args208⚠︎ from recoveryOS; nvram boot-args208⚠︎ then reads empty or approved.
  • P3
    Linux Root locked with passwd -l root107⚠︎ once the Phase 8 reboot came back clean and each admin passes sudo -v1⚠︎; from then on a failed boot recovers through the boot loader's kernel line:
    RHEL · SUSE → append rd.break145 to the kernel line (dracut), then mount -o remount,rw /sysroot; chroot /sysroot146 147⚠︎; SELinux hosts finish the repair with touch /.autorelabel148⚠︎ before exit3⚠︎, so files changed there get their labels at the next boot (slow on large disks).

    illumos Root becomes a role (OpenIndiana does this at install when it creates a user; OmniOS keeps root as a sign-in account) once the Phase 8 reboot came back clean, with the root shell kept open until a second admin session passes su - root2⚠︎ with root's vault password. First, grep -v '^#' /root/.ssh/authorized_keys⚠︎ and the owner list every job that signs in as root (backup pulls, zfs send pipelines, and configuration tools); each moves to a service account with the needed profile before root becomes a role, since a role takes sign-ins only through su, SSH keys included. A failed boot then recovers in single-user mode (boot -s153⚠︎ at the loader prompt), which still takes root's password (the Phase 6 PASSREQ read covers /etc/default/sulogin310):

  • P3
    Patch cadence and release upgrades:
    Debian → unattended-upgrades verified (unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug106⚠︎); Debian 12 hosts move to 13 before long-term support ends June 30, 2028.
    RHEL → the automatic timer verified; Fedora hosts move up before end of life (dnf system-upgrade download --releasever=<N>342⚠︎, then dnf system-upgrade reboot342⚠︎).
    SUSE → the 15.x online-update job or the 16.x os-update.timer343⚠︎ verified; SP6 hosts move to SP7 (zypper migration344⚠︎), and Leap 15.6 hosts move to Leap 16.0 with the distribution's migration tool.
    FreeBSD → freebsd-update cron71⚠︎ plus weekly pkg upgrade93⚠︎.
    OpenBSD → syspatch45⚠︎ and pkg_add -u95⚠︎ run on a schedule from root's crontab (syspatch -c45⚠︎ lists pending patches and suits cron). Errata reach the two most recent releases and package fixes the latest alone98, so 7.9 hosts move to 8.0 with sysupgrade99⚠︎ soon, and 8.0 hosts move to 8.1 within six months of its release. syspatch covers amd64, i386, and arm64; hosts on other architectures follow the source patches on the errata page. sysupgrade99⚠︎ reboots as soon as it finishes, so sysupgrade -n99⚠︎ stages the upgrade for a planned reboot.
    illumos → OmniOS: weekly pkg update92⚠︎, and a new stable release each May and November (Nov 2026: r151060 stable, r151058 until May 3, 2027, and r151054 LTS); r151056 left support on Nov 2, 2026, so its hosts move up first. Before the upgrade, sshd -t139⚠︎ passes (sshd starts on the new release once legacy options are gone), ipkg-branded zones are detached (zoneadm -z <zone> detach54⚠︎), and the session's evidence is copied off the host, since the new boot environment leaves out changes made after the update starts. Then beadm create <backup-name>12⚠︎, pkg set-publisher -r -O https://pkg.omnios.org/r151060/core omnios345⚠︎ (and the extra.omnios publisher the same way), pkg update -f -r --be-name=r15106092⚠︎, and a reboot. OpenIndiana Hipster rolls forward: pkg update92⚠︎, then a reboot into the new boot environment.
    Solaris → SRUs arrive monthly from the support repository that pkg publisher52⚠︎ names; pkg update -nv92⚠︎ previews the next one, and each lands in a new boot environment, live at the next reboot.
    macOS → the Phase 2 automatic-update settings verified; the 9 Nov 2026 security release346 covered macOS 27, 26, and 15, so a host on 14 or older goes on the plan as an upgrade.

Experimental: a starting point for your own judgment. Vendor documentation and your rehearsals decide. Rehearse on lab machines before you run these on a network you're responsible for.

Cisco IOS / IOS XE Takeover Checklist

Routers and Catalyst switches · IOS 15.x · IOS XE 17.x. For the network cell of a takeover team (a team lead plus one or more people per cell; a cell of three or more names a cell lead) inheriting a network whose last admin team left under a negligence finding.

Situation. Treat every secret the old team held as known to outsiders, and every setting as unreviewed. Lines that start with show, dir, copy, verify, clear, reload, more, terminal, configure, or guestshell, plus no monitor capture1⚠︎, run at the # prompt; the rest run in configure terminal2⚠︎. Indented lines run in the mode the line above opened.

Solo: edge router first, then core, then access switches; P1 lines in order, P2 when on schedule. Cell of two or more: split the devices in the Hosts bar, one person on the routers and the edge and the others on the switches; each person reads the line aloud, logs the change, and checks the → read-back. A cell of three or more names a cell lead, who sends the cell's roll-up to the team lead.

Key: P1 = inside the team clock · P2 = when on schedule · P3 = week-1 plan · → = expected read-back · <x> = your value · GUI+ = the GUI is faster here · ⚠︎ and an orange bar = untested on a real system: use with caution, at your own risk · a line without them = run cleanly on a real system.

Rules: evidence before change · a console session stays open for any VTY, ACL, AAA, or trunk change · keep every required link and service running · save each device after each phase · one change, one log line (time, device, change, old → new, undo).

1 · Access and evidence (read-only)

  • P1
    Console or out-of-band access to every device. A device without working credentials gets password recovery, inside the window.
  • P1
    GUI+ Turn on your terminal program's session logging (all output) before the first command; the log files are your evidence and your change record.
  • P1
    Evidence block, pasted per device:
    terminal length 03⚠︎show version4⚠︎show running-config5⚠︎show startup-config6⚠︎show users7⚠︎show ip interface brief8⚠︎show ip route9⚠︎show access-lists10⚠︎show logging11⚠︎show clock detail12⚠︎show cdp neighbors detail13⚠︎show archive14⚠︎dir15⚠︎
    Routershow ip nat translations · show crypto session · show interfaces summary16 17 18⚠︎
    Switchshow vlan brief · show interfaces trunk · show vtp status · show monitor session all19 20 21 22⚠︎
  • P1
    Copies before any change: copy running-config flash:takeover-before.cfg23⚠︎, and off the device copy running-config scp://<user>@<host>/<device>-before.cfg23⚠︎.
  • P1
    Running image matches the vendor's published hash: show version | include System image4⚠︎ → verify /sha512 <fs:image>24⚠︎ (install mode: each .pkg listed by more flash:packages.conf25⚠︎); IOS XE also show software authenticity running26⚠︎. A mismatch: collect evidence before any reload, isolate, and escalate.
  • P1
    Record signs of misuse (unknown privilege-15 users, outside hosts in ACLs, SNMP RW strings, tunnels, mirror sessions) and escalate per policy before fixing.

2 · Safety net and prepared blocks

  • P1
    Rollback timer before each remote change. Once per device: archive27⚠︎ → path flash:archive28⚠︎. Each session: configure terminal revert timer 102⚠︎, make the change, verify, then configure confirm29⚠︎ (test the timer once on one device). Backstop on any platform, while the change is unsaved: reload in 1030⚠︎ before, reload cancel30⚠︎ after (decline any save prompt).
  • P1
    GUI+ Fill in the Phase 3, 5, and 6 blocks once in a text editor (admin name, management subnets, NTP, syslog), then paste them per device; pasting beats retyping on every box.

3 · Cut off the old team

  • P1
    Live sessions: show users7⚠︎ → clear line vty <n>31⚠︎ for each session outside your team.
  • P1
    Accounts: show running-config | include ^username5⚠︎ → no username <u>32⚠︎ for each name off the approved list, privilege 15 first. Names such as cisco_tac_admin or cisco_support, or log lines from SEP_webui_wsma_http, point to the exploited web UI implant (CVE-2023-20198): isolate and escalate.
  • P1
    New secrets, hashed with scrypt (Type 9); the length floor goes first:
    security passwords min-length 1433⚠︎(classic IOS; IOS XE releases without it rely on vault-generated length)

4 · Hunt persistence

  • P1
    Scripts and schedulers: show running-config | section event manager|kron|scripting tcl5⚠︎ and show event manager policy registered53⚠︎ → no event manager applet <name>54⚠︎ for each unknown applet; no kron occurrence <name>55⚠︎ likewise.

    Guest Shell56 and hosted apps (IOS XE): show app-hosting list57⚠︎, show app-hosting detail appid guestshell57⚠︎, and show iox-service58⚠︎ → unknown apps are findings; guestshell destroy56⚠︎ and no iox59⚠︎ where the required list leaves hosted apps out.
  • P1
    Mirroring, captures, and tunnels: show monitor session all22⚠︎; show monitor capture22⚠︎; show ip interface brief | include Tunnel8⚠︎; show crypto session17⚠︎ → no monitor session <n>1⚠︎, no monitor capture <name>1⚠︎, and no interface Tunnel<n>60⚠︎ for each unknown one; stray .pcap files in flash are findings.
  • P1
    Routes, port forwards, and ACL permits match the required list: show running-config | include ^ip route|ip nat inside source static5⚠︎ and show access-lists10⚠︎ → remove orphans. Edit ACLs by sequence number (ip access-list extended <name>46⚠︎ → no <seq>), since no access-list <n>61⚠︎ deletes the whole list.
  • P1
    Odd listeners: IOS XE show control-plane host open-ports62⚠︎; every platform show running-config | include ip ssh port|ip http port|tftp-server|ip ftp5⚠︎ → nonstandard SSH ports (such as 22x22) or web ports, and any tftp-server63⚠︎ line (one serving the startup config is a known exploit trace), are findings.
  • P1
    Flash and boot: dir /recursive all-filesystems15⚠︎ → unexpected .tcl, .py, .pcap, .cfg, or extra images; show running-config | include boot system5⚠︎ → boots the image you verified.
  • P1
    AAA, SNMP trap, and syslog targets are yours (redirected TACACS+ hands every login to an outsider): show aaa servers64⚠︎; show running-config | include tacacs|radius|snmp-server host|logging host5⚠︎.

    DHCP pools hand out your gateway and DNS: show running-config | section ip dhcp pool5⚠︎.

6 · Shrink the attack surface

Announce port and edge-ACL changes at the firewall and ACL sync; users feel these first.

  • P1
    Legacy services off; dead sessions reaped (IP phones that need CDP keep it: use no cdp enable89⚠︎ on the other ports instead of no cdp run90⚠︎):

    vlan 999100⚠︎
    name PARKING101⚠︎

    switchport access vlan 999104⚠︎

  • P1

IOS XE below 17.9.10, 17.12.8, 17.15.6, 17.18.4, or 26.1.2 lacks the Aug 2026 hardening fixes; 16.12-only switches go on a replacement plan.

8 · Verify, freeze, hand off

From the freeze, verify and log only.

  • P1
    show running-config | include password|secret|community|http server|transport input|vstack5⚠︎ → hashed secrets, SSH, and SNMPv3 only.
  • P1
    show running-config | section line vty5⚠︎ → every range has login local42⚠︎ (or AAA), transport input ssh43⚠︎, transport output none43⚠︎, access-class49⚠︎, and exec-timeout65⚠︎.
  • P1
    IOS XE 17.18.2 and later: show system insecure configuration130⚠︎ → lists only features the owner kept on purpose.
  • P1
    From user PCs, every required service works (ping131⚠︎, tracert132⚠︎, app checks); from the management PC, SSH works.
  • P1
    Every device: the rollback timer is confirmed or cancelled, copy running-config startup-config23⚠︎ is done, and show startup-config6⚠︎ matches.
  • P1
    Hand off: terminal logs, vault entries, findings, and the week-1 plan.

Keep running

Approved accounts, required links, and third-party devices stay as they are. Monitoring moves to SNMPv3 rather than going dark. IP phones keep CDP on their ports. aaa new-model81⚠︎ follows a working local privilege-15 user. The native VLAN stays free of users. The management ACL lists every management subnet, or remote admins lose access.

Week-1 plan

  • P3
    AAA through TACACS+ or RADIUS with MFA, per-admin accounts, and command accounting.
  • P3
    Upgrades to fixed releases; scheduled config backups; flow export to a collector.
  • P3
    Control-plane policing, uRPF at the edge, dynamic ARP inspection, 802.1X on user ports; certificate-based VPN in place of pre-shared keys.
